regions.name: Mantinia
regions.summary: Mantinia is the high plateau of Arcadia in the central Peloponnese, around the town of Tripoli, and the home of Moschofilero, a pink-skinned, aromatic grape pressed pale into one of the freshest dry whites in Greece. An appellation since 1971, it requires at least 85% Moschofilero, the rest from the old local white grapes, and it is a white appellation above all. At 600 to 700 metres and more, with cold winters and one of the latest harvests in the country, it gives wine of low alcohol, bright acid and a perfume of rose, citrus and spice. Pour it as an aperitif or with shellfish and gentle spice; it smells like a Muscat but it is not one.

terroir.climate: Continental by Greek standards. The plateau lies inland and is ringed by mountains, so winters are cold, with frost and snow, springs come late and bring frost to the basin floor, and summer days are warm but the nights cool sharply. The season is long and cool for Greece, and Moschofilero is picked late, often well into October, one of the last harvests in the country. Autumn rain at picking is the vintage's great risk; in a cold, wet year the grape struggles to ripen, and in a warm one the wine gains weight but must keep its acid.
terroir.soils: Clay, sand and limestone in varying measure: sandy clay over limestone on the plateau floor and its gentle rises, poor and reasonably well drained, with deeper, heavier clay in the hollows and stonier ground towards the foot of the mountains. The lighter, poorer soils give Moschofilero its perfume and finesse; the richer floor gives bigger crops and simpler wine.
terroir.topography: A flat to gently rolling upland basin, the plateau of Tripoli, at roughly 600 to 700 metres, with vineyards climbing higher on its edges. Mount Mainalo rises to the west and other ranges close the basin on its other sides, so cold air pools on the floor at night. The ruins of ancient Mantinea lie on the plateau north of Tripoli and give the appellation its name.
terroir.water: No river or sea moderates the plateau. The basin has no outlet to the sea and drains through sinkholes in the limestone, and the absence of any large body of water is part of why its nights are so cold. The water that matters is winter rain and snow, held in the clay for the dry summer.

grapes.name: Moschofilero
grapes.styles: Pink to grey-skinned and aromatic, at least 85% of Mantinia: rose petal, orange blossom, lemon and a white pepper spice, light in body, low in alcohol and high in acid; pressed quickly to stay pale, or given skin contact for a pink wine outside the appellation.

grapes.name: Asproudes
grapes.styles: Not one grape but the local name for the old white varieties of the plateau, permitted up to 15% of a Mantinia beside Moschofilero.

grapes.name: Gewurztraminer
grapes.styles: Grown by a few plateau estates for regional whites, a natural neighbour to Moschofilero's perfume; it is never part of a wine labelled Mantinia.

wines.note: Pale, almost water-white with a faint pink glint: rose, lemon blossom, citrus and spice, light-bodied at around 12 per cent alcohol with crisp acid. Serve cold, at 7 to 9 degrees, as an aperitif or with oysters, crab, shrimp, raw fish and lightly spiced dishes, and drink it young.

Moschofilero's acid and perfume make a natural base for sparkling wine, by tank or by a second fermentation in bottle: floral, light and dry, a Greek aperitif, made under the appellation or as regional wine.
Moschofilero given a few hours on its coloured skins: pale salmon to pink, rose and strawberry, light and dry. It is sold as PGI Arcadia or PGI Peloponnese, because Mantinia is a white appellation.
A few estates age Moschofilero on its fine lees or in oak for texture: rounder and spicier, still fresh, for roast poultry, creamy shellfish dishes and soft cheeses.

made.viticulture: Most vineyards on the plateau are trained on wires, with older plots kept as bush vines, and the year is shaped by the cold. Spring frost on the basin floor threatens the young shoots, so sites with good air drainage on the gentle slopes are prized. Late ripening means a long hang time and an October harvest, when autumn rain can bring rot to the compact bunches. Moschofilero is vigorous and productive, and its quality falls quickly as the crop rises, so careful pruning and a moderate yield matter more than anything else. Skin colour varies from vineyard to vineyard and vine to vine, from grey to deep pink, because the grape exists in several forms, and the darker the skin, the more care is needed at pressing. Quality estates harvest by hand, often in the cool of the morning, to keep the aromatics. A warm, dry autumn gives the richest wine; a cool one gives a featherweight, sharply acid Mantinia.
made.winemaking: The aim is perfume and freshness. The grapes are chilled and then either pressed at once, for the palest white, or given a few hours of cold skin contact, which deepens the aroma and adds a blush that careful pressing and fining must manage. Fermentation is cool, in stainless steel, with selected or native yeasts, and the wine is usually bottled young without oak or malolactic conversion, to keep its acid and floral lift. Some producers age the wine on its fine lees for texture, and a few use oak for a fuller style. Sparkling wine is made by tank or by the traditional method from early-picked fruit. The same grapes given longer skin contact make the pink Moschofilero, and late-picked or dried grapes make an occasional sweet wine; both are sold outside the appellation.

law.classification: Mantinia was one of the first Greek appellations, decreed in 1971, and is today a protected designation of origin covering the plateau around Tripoli in Arcadia. The wine must contain at least 85% Moschofilero, the remainder from the old local white varieties known together as Asproudes. It is a white appellation: dry still white above all, and the specification also provides for a sparkling white. Rosé from Moschofilero, sweet wines and anything made from international varieties on the plateau are sold as PGI Arcadia or PGI Peloponnese. The national ageing terms exist but are rarely used, because Mantinia is a wine to drink young.
tiers: Mantinia PDO
Dry white, at least 85% Moschofilero with up to 15% Asproudes, from the delimited plateau of Arcadia: the classic style and the exam's answer.
Mantinia PDO sparkling
Sparkling white from the same grapes and zone, provided for by the specification; much Moschofilero sparkling wine is sold as regional wine instead.
PGI Arcadia and PGI Peloponnese
The regional wines of the same vineyards: Moschofilero rosé, sweet and late-harvest Moschofilero, and international varieties.

places.name: The plateau of Tripoli
places.note: The upland basin of central Arcadia at roughly 600 to 700 metres, the whole of the appellation's world: cold winters, cool nights, late harvests and pale, perfumed Moschofilero.

places.name: Tripoli
places.note: The capital of Arcadia and the plateau's market town, at the southern edge of the vineyard heart and the address of several Mantinia estates.

places.name: Ancient Mantinea (Mantineia)
places.note: The ruined classical city on the plateau north of Tripoli, scene of famous battles between the Greek city states, which lends the appellation its name.

places.name: Mount Mainalo
places.note: The mountain west of the plateau, nearly 2,000 metres high, whose bulk and snow make the basin colder; vineyards on its lower slopes are among the highest and latest in the zone.

places.name: Arcadia
places.note: The mountainous regional unit of the central Peloponnese that holds the plateau, and the name of the PGI under which the district's rosé, sweet and international wines are sold.

producers.name: Tselepos
producers.why: A family estate near Tripoli founded in 1989 whose Mantinia is a benchmark for the appellation, and whose Nemea estate, Driopi, ties the two Peloponnese answers together.

producers.name: Domaine Spiropoulos
producers.why: A long-established family estate on the plateau and an early convert to organic farming, a reference for traditional, fresh Mantinia.

producers.name: Boutari
producers.why: The old Naoussa house, founded in 1879, whose widely exported Moschofilero carried the grape to many lists abroad.

producers.name: Troupis
producers.why: A younger family winery on the plateau whose fresh, aromatic Moschofilero shows the modern style.

producers.name: Semeli
producers.why: A modern Peloponnese house with a Mantinia estate beside its Nemea one, so its range shows both of the region's exam answers.

exam: Moschofilero: pink-skinned and aromatic, at least 85% of Mantinia, the rest Asproudes.
The place: the Arcadian plateau around Tripoli in the central Peloponnese, roughly 600 to 700 metres; an appellation since 1971.
The climate: cold winters, cool nights, an October harvest, one of the latest in Greece, and why the wine is light and crisp.
The style: pale dry white of around 12 per cent alcohol, rose, citrus and spice; rosé and sweet wines are PGI Arcadia or PGI Peloponnese.
Service: cold and young, as an aperitif or with shellfish, raw fish and gentle spice.
traps: Moschofilero is not a Muscat, whatever the Moscho root and the floral nose suggest; it is a distinct Greek variety.
Mantinia and Nemea are both Peloponnese appellations, but Mantinia is high and white while Nemea is lower and red; the exam swaps them.
A pink Moschofilero is regional wine: the appellation is white, whatever the colour of the grape's skin.
Pink skin, white wine: like Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, Moschofilero must be pressed quickly to stay pale.
The appellation is spelt Mantinia, the ancient city Mantinea or Mantineia; they are one place under three spellings.

cards.f: Mantinia: the grape and its minimum
cards.b: Moschofilero, at least 85%; the rest Asproudes, the old local white grapes. Dry white above all, with a sparkling white provided for. An appellation since 1971.

cards.f: Where is Mantinia, and how high?
cards.b: The plateau of Tripoli in Arcadia, central Peloponnese, at roughly 600 to 700 metres, ringed by mountains with Mount Mainalo to the west.
Pale with a faint pink glint; rose, orange blossom, lemon, white pepper; light, around 12 per cent alcohol, crisp acid. Drink it young and cold.
No. The name and the perfume suggest one, but it is a distinct pink-skinned Greek variety; the Muscats of Greece are Muscat Blanc and Muscat of Alexandria.
Late, often well into October, one of the last in Greece. Autumn rain and rot are the danger at picking; spring frost on the basin floor is the other.

cards.f: Where does a Moschofilero rosé go?
cards.b: PGI Arcadia or PGI Peloponnese: Mantinia is a white appellation, so the pink wine from the same grape leaves it.
At 7 to 9 degrees, young, as an aperitif or with oysters, crab, shrimp, raw fish and gently spiced dishes; a fine answer for a guest who likes dry Riesling or Albariño.

questions.q: What minimum share of its principal grape must a Mantinia PDO white contain?
questions.exp: Mantinia must be at least 85% Moschofilero, the remainder from the old local white grapes called Asproudes; it is not a single-variety rule like Nemea's Agiorgitiko.

questions.q: In which regional unit of the Peloponnese does the Mantinia plateau lie?
questions.exp: Mantinia is the plateau of Tripoli in Arcadia, central Peloponnese. Corinthia holds Nemea, Achaea holds Patras with its Muscat and Mavrodaphne, and Messinia lies to the south-west.

questions.q: What colour is the skin of a ripe Moschofilero grape?
questions.exp: Moschofilero is pink to grey-skinned, like Pinot Gris, so it is pressed quickly for a pale white; with skin contact it makes a rosé sold as regional wine.

questions.q: Roughly how high does the Mantinia plateau lie?
questions.exp: The plateau of Tripoli lies at roughly 600 to 700 metres, with vineyards higher on its edges; the altitude and the inland position explain the cold nights and the late harvest.

questions.q: Which grape is the principal variety of the Mantinia PDO?
questions.exp: Mantinia is at least 85% Moschofilero, an aromatic grape pressed into a pale, floral, crisp dry white; despite its name and perfume it is not a member of the Muscat family.

questions.q: Which local term covers the old white varieties allowed up to 15% in a Mantinia?
questions.exp: Asproudes is the plateau's collective name for its old white grapes, which may make up the 15% of a Mantinia that is not Moschofilero.

questions.q: In which month is the Mantinia harvest usually brought in?
questions.exp: The cold, high plateau ripens Moschofilero late, usually in October, one of the last harvests in Greece; the islands pick in August, and July and December are out of the question for a dry white.

questions.q: Which description fits a young Mantinia in the glass?
opts: Pale and floral with crisp acidity
Deep gold and honeyed with low acidity
Amber and nutty from long cask ageing
questions.exp: Young Mantinia is pale, with rose, citrus and spice and crisp acid at low alcohol. Deep gold and honeyed suggests a sweet wine, pale ruby a red, and amber a long-aged sweet wine.

regions.name: Santorini
regions.summary: Santorini is a ring of volcanic islands in the southern Cyclades, north of Crete, and the home of Assyrtiko at its most intense: bone dry, saline, high in both acid and alcohol, and able to age for a decade or more. The vines grow on their own roots in ash and pumice where phylloxera has never survived, many of them woven into low kouloura baskets against the wind, and they drink the night's sea moisture rather than rain. The appellation, from 1971, covers the dry white, at least 85% Assyrtiko with Athiri and Aidani, its riper, oak-aged cousin Nykteri, and Vinsanto, the sun-dried sweet wine. It is the Greek white every guest has heard of.

terroir.climate: Hot, arid Mediterranean, with a few hundred millimetres of rain a year, almost all of it in winter, and long cloudless summers. Two forces make vines possible. The meltemi, the strong northerly wind of July and August, cools the island but batters and dries any exposed shoot. The humidity off the sea at night settles as dew and is soaked up by the porous pumice, feeding the roots through the drought. Fungal disease is rare in the dry, windy air, and the harvest comes early, usually in August.
terroir.soils: Volcanic through and through: layers of ash, pumice and lava from the island's eruptions, the greatest of them in the Late Bronze Age, which buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri. The local soil, called aspa, is sandy, porous and very poor, with almost no organic matter and no clay, so phylloxera, which needs clay to survive and spread, cannot live in it. The pumice holds the night's moisture like a sponge, and the volcanic rock is part of the wine's salt and stone.
terroir.topography: What remains of a volcano whose centre collapsed into the sea: a crescent of land, with Thirasia and Aspronisi completing the ring and the young volcanic islets of Nea and Palea Kameni in the middle of the flooded caldera. The cliffs on the inner side drop hundreds of metres to the water; the outer side slopes gently east and south to black sand beaches, and that slope is where most vines grow. The highest vineyards lie around Pyrgos, under Profitis Ilias, the island's one real mountain, a block of older limestone.
terroir.water: No rivers, no springs worth the name and almost no rain in the growing season: the sea is the island's only water, arriving as wind-borne humidity and night dew. The meltemi off the Aegean is the sea's other gift, cooling the vines and keeping disease away, at the price of salty, damaging gusts.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.styles: At least 85% of dry Santorini and 51% of Vinsanto: lemon, lime, flint, salt and smoke, piercing acid with real alcohol and weight, the rare white that keeps its acidity in a hot, dry climate.

grapes.name: Athiri
grapes.styles: A soft, lemony, low-acid white that may make up part of the remainder of a dry Santorini, adding perfume and roundness.

grapes.name: Aidani
grapes.styles: An aromatic white of flowers and herbs, the main partner of Assyrtiko in Vinsanto and a permitted minor share of the dry wine.

grapes.name: Mavrotragano
grapes.styles: A revived, nearly lost red of the island, deep, firm and spicy, made into serious dry red sold as PGI Cyclades.

grapes.name: Mandilaria
grapes.styles: A deeply coloured, tannic red grown on the island for reds and rosés sold as PGI Cyclades, since the appellation is white.

wines.note: Pale lemon with a green glint: lemon, lime, flint, smoke and sea salt, bone dry with searing acid, real body and 13 to 14.5 per cent alcohol. It opens over hours and ages for ten years and more towards honey and toast. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees with oysters, grilled fish, crab, shrimp and anything dressed with lemon and olive oil.

The traditional night-pressed wine, today a riper Santorini aged at least three months in oak: fuller and rounder, with toast and dried citrus over the salt. Serve a touch warmer with richer fish, lobster or roast poultry.

Assyrtiko and Aidani dried in the sun and aged at least two years in cask: amber to mahogany, with dried apricot, fig, raisin, coffee and orange peel, very sweet yet lifted by Assyrtiko's acid. Serve cool with blue cheese, nut tarts or chocolate, or on its own.

Single-vineyard and old-vine bottlings, some fermented with native yeast or aged on lees or in oak, all sold as Santorini: deeper in texture, with the same salt and acid, and the most age-worthy dry whites of the island.
Dry red from the revived local grape, sold as PGI Cyclades: deep colour, black fruit, spice and firm tannin with the island's freshness; a rarity and a fine talking point at the table.

made.viticulture: Santorini's vines are among the oldest living vineyards in Europe. Because phylloxera cannot survive in the ash, the vines grow on their own roots, and when a vine tires the grower cuts it back or layers it and lets the old root system throw new wood, so a root may be centuries old while the visible vine is young. The classic training is the kouloura: the canes are woven year after year into a low basket lying on the ground, with the grapes hanging inside, sheltered from the meltemi, from blown sand and from the sun. Some vines are kept as low bush vines, and a few modern plots are on wires. There is no irrigation; plantings are sparse to share the little water, and yields are tiny, a fraction of a mainland vineyard's. Harvest is by hand, often on the knees, usually in August, among the first in Greece. The threats are drought, wind and the pull of tourism on land and labour.
made.winemaking: Dry Santorini is made mostly in a protective style: grapes picked in the early morning, pressed, settled and fermented cool in stainless steel, often with some lees ageing and without malolactic conversion, so the wine keeps its acid and salt. A growing number of producers use native yeasts, older oak or long lees contact for texture. Nykteri takes its name from night work, when grapes were picked and pressed before dawn to escape the heat; today it is a riper wine with at least 13.5 per cent alcohol and at least three months in oak. Vinsanto is made from late-picked grapes laid out in the sun for a week or two until they shrivel, pressed to a thick must that ferments slowly to low alcohol and very high sugar, then aged at least two years in old casks, often far longer. The name is usually traced to the wine of Santorini traded through Venice, and in the nineteenth century much of it went to Russia for the Orthodox communion.

law.classification: Santorini was among the first Greek appellations, decreed in 1971, and is a protected designation of origin for wine from the island's own vineyards. The dry white must contain at least 85% Assyrtiko, the remainder Athiri and Aidani; older guides give 75%, the rule before an amendment of recent years. Nykteri is a protected term within the appellation for a riper dry white with at least 13.5% alcohol and at least three months in oak. Vinsanto is the sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, at least 51% Assyrtiko with Aidani the main partner, aged at least two years in oak. The appellation is white; reds, rosés and dry wines outside these rules are sold as PGI Cyclades.
tiers: Santorini PDO dry white
At least 85% Assyrtiko with Athiri and Aidani, from the island's own-rooted vines; oaked or unoaked, the wine every exam means by Santorini.
Nykteri
A protected term of the appellation: dry Santorini from riper grapes, at least 13.5% alcohol and at least three months in oak.
Vinsanto
The sweet wine of sun-dried grapes, at least 51% Assyrtiko with Aidani, aged at least two years in cask; one word, and never fortified.
PGI Cyclades
The regional wine of the island group: Mavrotragano and Mandilaria reds, rosés and whites outside the appellation's rules.

the sun-dried sweet wine of Santorini, written as one word

places.name: Pyrgos and the centre
places.note: The heart of the vineyard in the middle of the island, around Pyrgos, the highest village, below Profitis Ilias, with Megalochori, Episkopi Gonia and Exo Gonia on the slopes and plains around it.

places.name: Pyrgos
places.note: The highest village of Santorini, under the limestone peak of Profitis Ilias, with some of the coolest, windiest vineyards on the island and an old tradition of Vinsanto.

places.name: Megalochori
places.note: A village south-west of Pyrgos with old vineyards towards the caldera and several historic and modern wineries.

places.name: Episkopi Gonia
places.note: A village on the eastern plain below Pyrgos, home of old family estates and very old basket-trained vines.

places.name: Exo Gonia
places.note: A village on the slope between Pyrgos and the eastern coast, with vineyards falling towards the sea and several modern wineries.

places.name: The north
places.note: The narrowing arm of the crescent from Fira and Imerovigli on the caldera's edge to Oia at the tip, windswept and dry, with vineyards on the gentler outer slope and the sandy flats.

places.name: Oia
places.note: The village at the northern tip of the island, with vineyards on its exposed slopes and flats and one of the island's most celebrated estates.

places.name: Fira and Imerovigli
places.note: The island's capital and its neighbour on the caldera's rim, with vineyards behind them on the plain falling east towards the sea.

places.name: Akrotiri and the south
places.note: The southern arm of the crescent, around the buried Bronze Age town of Akrotiri and the village of Emporio, flatter and hotter, with wide vineyards of old baskets.

places.name: Akrotiri
places.note: The south-western peninsula and its village, whose name the excavated Bronze Age town under the ash now carries, with exposed vineyards facing the wind and the caldera.

places.name: Emporio
places.note: The largest village of the south, on the plain below Profitis Ilias, surrounded by old basket-trained vineyards.

places.name: Thirasia
places.note: The smaller island on the western side of the caldera, a fragment of the old volcano's rim, with a few basket-trained vineyards of its own on the same ash.

places.name: Profitis Ilias
places.note: The island's highest point, at about 570 metres, a block of older limestone that the volcano built around; it shelters the vineyards of Pyrgos and Exo Gonia.

producers.name: Domaine Sigalas
producers.why: An estate at Oia in the north, founded in 1991, whose Santorini and single-vineyard Kavalieros set a modern standard for site-driven Assyrtiko.

producers.name: Estate Argyros
producers.why: A family estate at Episkopi Gonia, founded in 1903, with some of the island's oldest own-rooted vines; its Cuvée Monsignori and long-aged Vinsanto are benchmarks.

producers.name: Gaia Wines
producers.why: Founded in 1994, with a Santorini winery whose Thalassitis showed the world sharp, saline Assyrtiko and whose native-yeast wines followed; also a leading Nemea house.

producers.name: Hatzidakis
producers.why: A small organic estate at Pyrgos, known for powerful old-vine Assyrtiko, Nykteri and Mavrotragano from a cellar cut into the pumice.

producers.name: Gavalas
producers.why: One of the island's old family wineries, at Megalochori, keeping traditional Nykteri, Vinsanto and rare local grapes alive.

producers.name: Santo Wines
producers.why: The union of the island's growers' cooperatives, founded in 1947, which takes the grapes of many smallholders and makes the full range from dry Assyrtiko to Vinsanto.

producers.name: Boutari
producers.why: The Naoussa house, among the first mainland producers to build a modern winery on the island, at Megalochori.

exam: Assyrtiko: at least 85% of dry Santorini, with Athiri and Aidani; at least 51% of Vinsanto.
The vineyard: own-rooted vines in volcanic ash and pumice, no phylloxera because there is no clay, kouloura baskets against the meltemi.
Water: almost no summer rain; night humidity and dew soaked up by the pumice.
The three wines: dry Santorini, Nykteri with oak, and Vinsanto from sun-dried grapes aged at least two years in cask.
The place: southern Cyclades, north of Crete; a caldera left by the Bronze Age eruption that buried Akrotiri.
The glass: bone dry, high acid, saline and flinty, with alcohol and weight; one of the great ageing whites of a hot climate.
An appellation since 1971 and white only; Mavrotragano and other reds are PGI Cyclades.
traps: Vinsanto, one word, is Santorini's; Vin Santo, two words, is Tuscany's; neither is fortified.
Older guides give 75% Assyrtiko for dry Santorini; the current rule is at least 85%.
The kouloura protects against wind, sand and sun; it is not a defence against phylloxera, which the ash keeps away by itself.
Nykteri means of the night, from the old night picking and pressing; today it means riper and oak-aged, not harvested after dark.
Vinsanto is made from white grapes, though it ages to a deep amber, almost red-brown colour; it is not a red wine.
Assyrtiko grows on the mainland and on other islands too; only wine from the Santorini group itself may carry the name Santorini.

cards.b: At least 85% Assyrtiko, the remainder Athiri and Aidani. Older guides give 75%, the rule before an amendment of recent years.

cards.f: Why is there no phylloxera on Santorini?
cards.b: The volcanic ash and pumice hold no clay, so the louse cannot survive. The vines grow on their own roots, some root systems centuries old.

cards.f: The kouloura: what it is and why
cards.b: A vine whose canes are woven into a low basket on the ground, the grapes inside, sheltered from the meltemi wind, blown sand and the sun.

cards.f: How do Santorini's vines get water?
cards.b: Hardly any summer rain: night humidity and dew off the sea, soaked up by the porous pumice, and the winter rain held in the ground.

cards.f: Nykteri: the name and the rule
cards.b: Of the night, from the old night picking and pressing. Today a riper dry Santorini with at least 13.5% alcohol and at least three months in oak.
At least 51% Assyrtiko with Aidani, sun-dried, fermented to very high sugar, aged at least two years in cask; never fortified. One word, unlike Tuscany's Vin Santo.
Pale lemon; lemon, lime, flint, smoke, sea salt; bone dry, searing acid, real body and alcohol. Ages ten years and more towards honey and toast.

cards.f: What made the landscape of Santorini?
cards.b: A Late Bronze Age eruption: the volcano's centre collapsed into the sea, leaving a caldera ringed by Santorini, Thirasia and Aspronisi, and the ash buried the town of Akrotiri.
At 8 to 10 degrees with oysters, crab, shrimp, grilled fish, lemon and olive oil; decant an old one. Vinsanto cool with blue cheese or nut desserts.

questions.q: What minimum share of Assyrtiko does a dry PDO Santorini require?
questions.exp: Dry Santorini needs at least 85% Assyrtiko, the rest Athiri and Aidani. 51% is the Vinsanto minimum, and 75% is the older rule some guides still print.

questions.q: Why can phylloxera not survive in Santorini's vineyards?
opts: The volcanic soil holds no clay
The vines are grafted on resistant rootstock
The island is too cold in winter
The vineyards are flooded each winter
questions.exp: Phylloxera needs clay to live and move, and Santorini's ash and pumice hold none, so the vines grow on their own roots. They are not grafted, the winters are mild, and nothing is flooded on this dry island.

questions.q: What is a kouloura on Santorini?
questions.exp: The kouloura is a vine whose canes are woven into a low basket on the ground to shelter the grapes from the meltemi, blown sand and the sun; a cave winery is a kanava.

questions.q: What name is given to the riper, oak-aged style of dry Santorini, once pressed at night?
questions.exp: Nykteri means of the night, from the old night harvest and pressing; today it requires riper grapes, at least 13.5% alcohol and at least three months in oak.

questions.q: How is the sweetness of Vinsanto achieved?
questions.exp: Vinsanto's grapes are laid in the sun to shrivel, then fermented and aged at least two years in cask; it is never fortified. Spirit makes Samos Vin Doux, noble rot makes Tokaji, and frozen grapes make ice wine.

questions.q: Which wind shapes the training of Santorini's vines?
questions.exp: The meltemi, the strong summer northerly of the Aegean, is why vines are woven into low kouloura baskets. The sirocco blows hot from Africa, the mistral down the Rhône valley, and the bora on the Adriatic.

questions.q: Which white grape is Assyrtiko's main partner in Vinsanto?
questions.exp: Vinsanto is at least 51% Assyrtiko, with Aidani, an aromatic white of flowers and herbs, as the main partner; Athiri more often softens the dry wine.

questions.q: Under which designation is a dry red Mavrotragano from Santorini sold?
questions.exp: The Santorini appellation covers white wines only, so Mavrotragano and Mandilaria reds go out as PGI Cyclades. Paros is its own appellation, and PGI Crete belongs to the larger island to the south.

regions.name: Crete
regions.summary: Crete, the largest Greek island and the most southerly wine region in the country, keeps its own grapes and seven appellations. The whites are Vilana, the old staple of Peza, and Vidiano, the rising star of apricot and herbs, with Thrapsathiri, Dafni, Plyto and the aromatic Malvasia beside them. The reds are soft, spicy Kotsifali, dark, tannic Mandilaria and pale, early Liatiko, which also makes the island's sweet red. Five appellations lie in Heraklion, Peza, Archanes, Dafnes, Handakas-Candia and Malvasia Handakas-Candia, and two in Lasithi, Sitia and Malvasia Sitia. Mountains, altitude and north-facing slopes make fresh wine possible this far south.

terroir.climate: Hot Mediterranean, the warmest of the Greek wine regions: long, dry summers, mild, wet winters, and more rain in the west than in the dry east. The island's spine of high mountains catches the winter rain and shelters the northern slopes from the hot, dusty winds that blow off Africa across the Libyan Sea, while the summer northerlies off the Aegean cool the side that faces them. Altitude is the great moderator: the best vineyards sit several hundred metres up, where the nights are cool enough to hold acid.
terroir.soils: Limestone and marl over clay across much of the vineyard, with schist and clay in places and sandy loam on the coastal plains. The limestone and marl of the inland slopes drain well and give structure and freshness; the deeper clays hold water through the long drought; the sandy coastal soils make lighter, simpler wine.
terroir.topography: A long, narrow, mountainous island, about 260 kilometres from west to east, with four main massifs: the White Mountains in the west, Psiloritis, the ancient Mount Ida and the highest peak at almost 2,500 metres, in the centre, Dikti further east, and the mountains of Sitia at the eastern end. Most vineyards lie on the northern side: on the hills and plateaus south of Heraklion around Peza and Archanes, at the foot of the mountains west of the city at Dafnes, and in the hills of Sitia in the east. Chania and Rethymno in the west have regional wines of their own.
terroir.water: The sea surrounds and tempers everything: the Aegean to the north, whose breezes cool the north-facing vineyards, and the Libyan Sea to the south, across which the hot southern winds arrive. Rivers are few and seasonal, and in the dry east drought-tolerant old varieties and careful water use matter most.

grapes.name: Vilana
grapes.styles: The traditional white of Heraklion, alone in Peza white and the lead of Sitia white: light, lemony, floral and soft, at its best fresh and young.

grapes.name: Vidiano
grapes.styles: Rescued from near extinction in recent decades and now the island's flagship white: apricot, peach, herbs and a chalky, mineral texture with good acid and body; it makes serious dry whites that age.

grapes.name: Kotsifali
grapes.styles: The island's most important red: soft, spicy and high in alcohol but light in colour and tannin, the lead grape of Peza and Archanes red, blended with Mandilaria for colour and grip.

grapes.name: Mandilaria
grapes.styles: Deep in colour, high in tannin and low in alcohol, harsh on its own: the partner that gives Kotsifali colour and structure.

grapes.name: Liatiko
grapes.styles: An ancient, early-ripening red, pale and soft, the grape of Dafnes and Sitia red and of the island's traditional sweet red from sun-dried grapes.

grapes.name: Thrapsathiri
grapes.styles: A local white of good body, the partner of Vilana in Sitia white.

grapes.name: Dafni
grapes.styles: A revived local white named after the bay laurel, whose leaf it smells of: herbal, aromatic and unusual.

grapes.name: Plyto
grapes.styles: A near-lost white saved by a Heraklion estate: light, lemony and high in acid.

grapes.name: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica
grapes.styles: The aromatic Malvasia grown on Crete, linked by name to the island's medieval Malmsey trade and part of the blend of the sweet whites of its two Malvasia appellations.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Grown widely on the island for regional reds and blends with Kotsifali, where it adds colour and spice.

wines.note: Vilana alone: pale, light, with lemon, green apple and white flowers and soft acid; a simple, refreshing island white for meze, salads and grilled fish, drunk young.

The modern Cretan white, often sold as PGI Crete: apricot, peach, chamomile and herbs over a chalky, mineral texture, medium to full in body with good acid; lees-aged and oaked versions age well. Serve with lobster, roast chicken or fish in a rich sauce.
Kotsifali with Mandilaria: medium-bodied, with red cherry, dried herbs and sweet spice, warm alcohol and moderate tannin. Serve slightly cool with lamb, goat, grilled pork and tomato dishes.

Liatiko-led, pale ruby to garnet, with strawberry, dried cherry, earth and spice and a soft tannin; it ages towards dried fruit and leather. A light red for game birds, mushrooms and herb-scented dishes.

Liatiko from sun-dried grapes, made sweet under the Dafnes and Sitia appellations: raisin, fig, dried cherry and spice, the heir of the island's ancient sweet reds. Serve cool with nuts, dried fruit and cheese.
Sweet whites from a blend that includes the aromatic Malvasia, reviving the name of the medieval Malmsey trade: apricot, orange peel, honey and spice. Serve with blue cheese or nut desserts.

made.viticulture: Phylloxera reached Crete only in the 1970s, long after the mainland, and the replanting on resistant rootstocks that followed swept away much of the old vineyard and many old varieties; the rescue of grapes such as Vidiano, Dafni and Plyto is the modern reply. Vines are bush-trained on the older, drier plots and on wires in the newer vineyards, and growers choose altitude and north-facing slopes to temper the heat. Drought is the constant risk, especially in the east, and water is used carefully where it is available. The harvest is early, beginning in August, and quick: the whites first, Liatiko among the earliest reds and Mandilaria later. Wind keeps fungal disease low, so organic farming is easier here than in much of Greece. The great choice is site: altitude for whites and freshness, lower and warmer ground for sweet Liatiko.
made.winemaking: Cretan winemaking modernised from the 1990s, when temperature control and stainless steel came to the old cooperatives and a new generation of estates. The whites are fermented cool in steel and bottled young; Vidiano is more and more often given lees ageing, skin contact or oak to build its texture, and it takes to all three. The classic reds blend Kotsifali, for alcohol and spice, with Mandilaria, for colour and tannin, the two fermented together or apart and aged in tank or oak. Liatiko, pale and soft, is made into light dry reds, older-style oak-aged reds that develop for years, and sweet wine from grapes dried in the sun before pressing. The two Malvasia appellations revive the island's old sweet whites. International grapes, Syrah above all, are blended with the local reds under PGI Crete.

law.classification: Crete has seven protected designations of origin. Five lie in the Heraklion regional unit: Peza, for white from Vilana alone and red from Kotsifali with Mandilaria; Archanes, a red from the same two grapes; Dafnes, a dry and sweet red led by Liatiko; Handakas-Candia; and Malvasia Handakas-Candia. Two lie in Lasithi in the east: Sitia, for white from Vilana with Thrapsathiri, red from Liatiko with a little Mandilaria, and sweet Liatiko; and Malvasia Sitia, a sweet white. Peza, Archanes, Dafnes and Sitia are the old appellations; the Handakas and Malvasia names are later. Much of the island's best modern wine, Vidiano above all, is sold as PGI Crete or under the district PGIs.

Heraklion: white from Vilana alone; red from Kotsifali with Mandilaria, Kotsifali the larger share.
Archanes PDO
Heraklion, around the town of Archanes: red only, Kotsifali with Mandilaria.
Dafnes PDO
Heraklion, west of the city: dry and sweet red led by Liatiko.
Sitia PDO
Lasithi in the east: white from Vilana with Thrapsathiri, red from Liatiko with a little Mandilaria, and sweet Liatiko.
Handakas-Candia, Malvasia Handakas-Candia and Malvasia Sitia
The later appellations: a Heraklion PDO named for the city's medieval names, and two sweet white Malvasia appellations from a blend that includes the aromatic Malvasia.
PGI Crete and the district PGIs
Island-wide and district regional wines: Vidiano, blends with Syrah and other international grapes, rosé.

places.name: Heraklion
places.note: The central regional unit around the island's capital, holding five of the seven appellations and most of the vineyard, on the hills and plateaus south and west of the city.

places.name: Peza
places.note: The hills and plateau south-east of Heraklion, a few hundred metres up, the island's best-known appellation: Vilana white and Kotsifali with Mandilaria red, from a large cooperative and many estates.

places.name: Archanes
places.note: The town and slopes south of Heraklion below Mount Giouchtas, red only, Kotsifali with Mandilaria, near the Minoan wine press of Vathypetro.

places.name: Dafnes
places.note: The villages west of Heraklion at the foot of the mountains, for Liatiko-led red, dry and sweet.

places.name: Handakas-Candia
places.note: An appellation of the Heraklion district named for the city's Arab and Venetian names, with a Malvasia appellation of the same name for sweet white.

places.name: Vathypetro
places.note: A Minoan villa south of Archanes holding one of the oldest known wine presses in Europe, from the Bronze Age, proof of more than three thousand years of Cretan wine.

places.name: Lasithi and Sitia
places.note: The eastern end of the island and its driest part, with the appellations of Sitia and Malvasia Sitia in the hills around the town of Sitia, some vineyards high on its plateaus.

places.name: Sitia
places.note: White from Vilana with Thrapsathiri, red from Liatiko with a little Mandilaria, and sweet Liatiko, from the hills and plateaus of the far east.

places.name: Malvasia Sitia
places.note: A sweet white appellation in the same district, reviving the island's Malmsey from a blend that includes the aromatic Malvasia.

places.name: Chania and Rethymno
places.note: The wetter, greener west under the White Mountains, with no appellation but regional wines of character, Romeiko as the local red, and a new generation of estates working with local and Rhône grapes.

producers.name: Lyrarakis
producers.why: A family house in the hills of Heraklion, known for rescuing near-lost white grapes such as Plyto and Dafni and for its Vidiano.

producers.name: Douloufakis
producers.why: A family winery at Dafnes whose Vidiano and Liatiko showed what the island's old grapes could do.

producers.name: Domaine Economou
producers.why: A small estate in the hills of Sitia, known for traditional, long-aged Liatiko reds released years after the vintage.

producers.name: Alexakis
producers.why: A Heraklion house that helped carry Vidiano and Kotsifali onto export lists.

producers.name: Manousakis
producers.why: An estate near Chania in the west, known for its Nostos wines from Rhône grapes and for the local red Romeiko.

exam: Crete's grapes: Vilana and Vidiano white; Kotsifali, Mandilaria and Liatiko red.
The seven PDOs: Peza, Archanes, Dafnes, Handakas-Candia and Malvasia Handakas-Candia in Heraklion; Sitia and Malvasia Sitia in Lasithi.
The pairings: Kotsifali with Mandilaria at Peza and Archanes, Liatiko at Dafnes and Sitia, Vilana alone in Peza white.
Vidiano as the rising white, rescued from near extinction and mostly sold as PGI Crete.
History: Minoan wine at Vathypetro, the Venetian Malmsey trade of Candia, phylloxera arriving only in the 1970s.
Sweet Liatiko from sun-dried grapes under Dafnes and Sitia, and the two sweet Malvasia appellations.
traps: Kotsifali gives alcohol and spice but little colour; Mandilaria gives colour and tannin. The exam swaps their roles.
Vidiano is the island's star white, yet most of it is PGI Crete rather than one of the appellations.
Archanes is red only; Peza makes both white and red.
Dafnes the appellation is not Dafni the grape: one is a place for Liatiko, the other a bay-scented white.
Phylloxera reached Crete only in the 1970s; Santorini, not Crete, is the island it never reached.
Candia is Heraklion's Venetian name, and Malvasia di Candia Aromatica is the island's grape; Madeira's Malmsey is a different wine with a shared trade name.

cards.b: Heraklion: Peza, Archanes, Dafnes, Handakas-Candia, Malvasia Handakas-Candia. Lasithi: Sitia, Malvasia Sitia.

cards.f: Kotsifali and Mandilaria: who brings what?
cards.b: Kotsifali: alcohol, softness, spice, little colour. Mandilaria: deep colour and tannin, low alcohol. Blended at Peza and Archanes, Kotsifali the larger share.
White from Vilana alone; red from Kotsifali with Mandilaria. South-east of Heraklion, a few hundred metres up.
Pale, soft, early-ripening red. Leads Dafnes and Sitia red, with a little Mandilaria at Sitia; sun-dried for the island's sweet red.
Crete's rising white, saved from near extinction: apricot, peach, herbs, chalky texture, good acid. Mostly sold as PGI Crete; ages well with lees or oak.

cards.f: Crete's wine history in three marks
cards.b: Minoan press at Vathypetro in the Bronze Age; the Venetian Malmsey trade of Candia; phylloxera only in the 1970s, then replanting and the rescue of old grapes.

cards.f: What tempers the heat on Crete?
cards.b: Altitude, several hundred metres up; north-facing slopes cooled by Aegean breezes; the mountain spine sheltering them from hot winds off Africa.

cards.f: Serving Cretan wine at the table
cards.b: Vilana with meze and grilled fish; Vidiano with lobster or roast chicken; Kotsifali reds slightly cool with lamb; sweet Liatiko with nuts and cheese.

questions.q: Which grape gives the red wine of Peza most of its colour and tannin?
questions.exp: Mandilaria is deep in colour and tannic and is blended with Kotsifali, which brings alcohol and spice but little colour. Liatiko leads Dafnes and Sitia, and Romeiko is the red of Chania.

questions.q: Which grape alone makes the white wine of Peza?
questions.exp: Peza white is Vilana alone. Vidiano is the rising white usually sold as PGI Crete, Thrapsathiri partners Vilana in Sitia, and Assyrtiko belongs to Santorini.

questions.q: Which grape leads the red wines of Dafnes?
questions.exp: Dafnes, west of Heraklion, is a Liatiko appellation for dry and sweet red. Kotsifali and Mandilaria make Peza and Archanes, and Agiorgitiko belongs to Nemea.

questions.q: Which white grape, rescued from near extinction, has become Crete's flagship white?
questions.exp: Vidiano, saved over recent decades, gives apricot, herbs and a chalky texture with good acid and now leads the island's white revival, mostly as PGI Crete.

questions.q: In which regional unit do Sitia and Malvasia Sitia lie?
questions.exp: Sitia and Malvasia Sitia are in Lasithi, the dry east. The other five Cretan appellations are in Heraklion, while Chania and Rethymno have regional wines only.

questions.q: How many PDO appellations does Crete hold?
questions.exp: Crete has seven: Peza, Archanes, Dafnes, Handakas-Candia and Malvasia Handakas-Candia in Heraklion, and Sitia and Malvasia Sitia in Lasithi.

questions.q: In which decade did phylloxera reach Crete?
questions.exp: Phylloxera arrived on Crete only in the 1970s, about eighty years after it reached the mainland, and the replanting swept away many old varieties; Santorini's ash has never let it in.

questions.q: Which Cretan appellation makes red wine only, from Kotsifali with Mandilaria?
questions.exp: Archanes, around the town south of Heraklion, is red only, Kotsifali with Mandilaria. Peza uses the same two grapes for its red but also makes a white from Vilana, and Dafnes is a Liatiko appellation.

regions.name: Kefalonia
regions.summary: Kefalonia, the largest of the Ionian islands, off the west coast of mainland Greece, is the home of Robola, a white of lemon, flint and smoke grown on bare limestone up the slopes of Mount Ainos, some of it still on its own roots. The island holds three appellations: Robola of Kefalonia for the dry white, and the sweet Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia and Muscat of Kefalonia. Its Venetian and British past, its earthquakes and its rare local grapes, Vostilidi, Zakynthino and Tsaousi among them, make it a small region with a long memory. Robola is the answer the exam wants, and it is not the Ribolla Gialla of Friuli.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean with an Ionian accent: mild, wet winters, wetter than those of the Aegean islands because the west of Greece catches the rain of the westerly storms, and hot, dry, sunny summers. The sea moderates both seasons, and altitude on Mount Ainos brings cool nights to the higher vineyards, which pick later. Winter rain stored in the limestone carries the vines through the summer drought, and breezes off the Ionian keep the canopy dry.
terroir.soils: Limestone above all: bare white scree, broken rock and karst with little true soil, the vines rooting deep into fissures in the stone. Phylloxera made slow progress in this poor, stony ground and some old vines still grow on their own roots. Pockets of clay and marl on the lower slopes and valley floors give fuller wines; the scree gives the tense, stony Robola the island is known for.
terroir.topography: A mountainous, deeply indented island of bays and peninsulas, dominated by Mount Ainos, over 1,600 metres, its upper slopes clothed in the island's own fir. The heart of Robola lies in the Omala valley, a high basin below Ainos, and on the slopes around it; other vineyards lie on the Paliki peninsula in the west around Lixouri, and in the hills near the capital, Argostoli, across the bay.
terroir.water: The Ionian Sea surrounds the island and tempers it, and the deep bay of Argostoli and Lixouri cuts into its west. Rivers are few: the karst swallows the rain and returns it through caves, springs and sinkholes, a sign of how quickly the stony ground drains.

grapes.name: Robola
grapes.styles: The island's great white and the only grape of Robola of Kefalonia: lemon, lime, flint and smoke over a lean, high-acid frame, with a stony, saline finish; the best age for several years.

grapes.name: Mavrodaphne
grapes.styles: The black laurel grape, made into the fortified sweet Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia and, more and more, into a dry red of dark fruit and spice.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: The small-berried Muscat of the island's sweet Muscat of Kefalonia appellation, grapey, floral and orange-scented.

grapes.name: Vostilidi
grapes.styles: A rare local white, rich and aromatic with a golden colour, revived by a few estates as a dry wine.

grapes.name: Zakynthino
grapes.styles: A white named for neighbouring Zakynthos, soft and herbal, made by a few Kefalonia estates.

grapes.name: Tsaousi
grapes.styles: An old local white, also eaten as a table grape, soft and low in acid, used in island blends.

wines.note: Pale lemon, with lemon, lime, white flowers, flint and a smoky edge, lean and high in acid with a stony, saline finish. Serve at 8 to 10 degrees with grilled fish, shellfish, octopus and the island's meat pie; the best keep for five years and more.
The fortified sweet red, aged in cask: raisin, prune, coffee, chocolate and spice. Serve cool with chocolate, dried fruit or nuts, as one would a tawny port.
Sweet white Muscat, grapey, floral and orange-scented, a cool dessert wine for fruit tarts, almond pastries and soft cheeses.
A modern dry red from the same black grape, sold as regional wine: dark fruit, laurel, pepper and cocoa, firm and fresh; for grilled lamb and game.
Rare local whites made dry by a few estates and sold as regional wine: rich, golden, herbal and spicy, a discovery for an adventurous table.

made.viticulture: Kefalonia's vineyards are small, scattered and hard to work: terraces and stony slopes where machines cannot go, many abandoned after the earthquake of 1953 emptied the villages and sent their people abroad. Robola is mostly grown as low bush vines, some still own-rooted in the scree, with very low yields from the poor limestone; newer plantings are on wires. The vineyards of the Omala valley and the slopes of Ainos are among the higher ones in the Ionian, so Robola ripens slowly and is picked in September with its acid intact. Winter rain is ample and the summer dry, so disease is manageable with care, though the wetter climate makes mildew a greater threat than in the Aegean. A growers' cooperative in the Omala valley gathers the grapes of many smallholders, and the estates farm their own plots, several of them organically or biodynamically.
made.winemaking: Robola is made to keep its tension: picked by hand, pressed gently, settled and fermented cool in stainless steel, usually without oak or malolactic conversion, and bottled within a year. Some producers age it on fine lees for texture, and a few experiment with skin contact, native yeasts or barrels. The sweet wines follow the tradition shared with Patras across the water: Mavrodaphne is fortified with grape spirit to stop its fermentation and keep its sugar, then aged in cask, often for years, and Muscat is made sweet in the same tradition. The modern dry Mavrodaphne is fermented fully dry and aged in oak, and the rare local whites are made dry with little intervention.

law.classification: Kefalonia has three protected designations of origin. Robola of Kefalonia is the dry white from Robola alone, grown on the island's limestone, with the Omala valley and the slopes of Mount Ainos at its heart. Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia is a fortified sweet red, and Muscat of Kefalonia a sweet white from Muscat Blanc; both belong to the family of sweet appellations that once carried the old OPE seal, while Robola carried the dry appellation seal, OPAP. Everything else, the dry Mavrodaphne, the rare local whites, the rosés and the international grapes, is sold as regional wine. The national Reserve terms exist but are rarely seen, since Robola is drunk within a few years.
tiers: Robola of Kefalonia PDO
Dry white from 100% Robola, grown on the island's limestone: the appellation the exam asks.
Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia PDO
Fortified sweet red from Mavrodaphne, aged in cask: the island sister of Mavrodaphne of Patras across the water.
Muscat of Kefalonia PDO
Sweet white Muscat from Muscat Blanc.
Regional wine
The PGI wines of the island and the Ionian: dry Mavrodaphne, Vostilidi, Zakynthino, Tsaousi and international varieties.
labels: the grape, part of the appellation's name

places.name: The Omala valley
places.note: A high basin in the centre of the island below Mount Ainos, the heart of Robola and home of the growers' cooperative, its vineyards on limestone at altitude, cool at night and late to ripen.

places.name: Mount Ainos
places.note: The island's mountain, over 1,600 metres, a national park clothed in Kefalonian fir; vineyards on its lower slopes give the most tense and stony Robola.

places.name: Paliki and Lixouri
places.note: The western peninsula and its town across the bay from Argostoli, with lower, warmer vineyards and estates working the rare local whites and dry Mavrodaphne.

places.name: Argostoli
places.note: The island's capital on its sheltered bay, with vineyards and estates in the hills around it.

places.name: The Ionian Islands
places.note: The island chain off the west coast of Greece, Corfu, Lefkada, Ithaca, Kefalonia and Zakynthos among them, Venetian until 1797 and British from 1815 to 1864; Kefalonia is the wine island the exam names.

producers.name: Gentilini
producers.why: One of the first modern estates on the island, near Argostoli, whose Robola helped restore Kefalonia's reputation abroad.

producers.name: Sclavos
producers.why: A family estate on the Paliki peninsula farming biodynamically, known for low-intervention Robola, Vostilidi and Mavrodaphne.

producers.name: Orealios Gaea (the Robola Cooperative of Kefalonia)
producers.why: The growers' cooperative in the Omala valley, which makes much of the island's Robola and is the bottling a server meets most often.

producers.name: Haritatos
producers.why: An estate near Lixouri reviving Vostilidi and other rare local grapes as dry wines.

exam: Robola: the only grape of Robola of Kefalonia, a lean, lemony, stony dry white grown on limestone.
The three PDOs: Robola of Kefalonia dry, Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia fortified, Muscat of Kefalonia sweet.
The place: the largest Ionian island, off the west coast of mainland Greece; Mount Ainos and the Omala valley.
Soil and roots: bare limestone scree and karst, low bush vines, some still own-rooted.
The sweet links: Mavrodaphne and Muscat, as at Patras across the water.
traps: Robola is not Ribolla Gialla of Friuli; the names look alike and older books linked them, but they are different grapes.
Kefalonia is Ionian, in the west; Santorini and Samos are Aegean islands, in the south and east.
Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia is not Mavrodaphne of Patras: one grape, two appellations, one on the island and one on the mainland.
Robola is the dry white; the island's sweet wines are Mavrodaphne and Muscat, not a sweet Robola.
Kefalonia's soils are limestone, not volcanic; the stony, smoky note comes from limestone and grape, not from ash as on Santorini.

cards.b: Robola of Kefalonia, dry white; Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia, fortified sweet red; Muscat of Kefalonia, sweet white.
Pale lemon; lemon, lime, white flowers, flint and smoke; lean, high acid, a stony, saline finish. Drink cold within a few years, with fish and shellfish.
The Omala valley and the slopes of Mount Ainos, on bare limestone scree and karst, mostly low bush vines, some still on their own roots.

cards.f: Are Robola and Ribolla Gialla the same grape?
cards.b: Different grapes. The names look alike and older references linked them through the Venetians; Robola is Kefalonia's, Ribolla Gialla belongs to Friuli and Slovenia.
The largest Ionian island, off the west coast of mainland Greece, north of Zakynthos; Venetian until 1797, British from 1815 to 1864.
Vostilidi, golden and aromatic; Zakynthino, soft and herbal; Tsaousi, soft and low in acid, also a table grape. Revived by a few estates as dry regional wine.

cards.f: Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia at the table
cards.b: A fortified sweet red aged in cask: raisin, prune, coffee, chocolate. Serve cool with chocolate desserts, dried fruit or nuts, as one would a tawny port.

questions.q: Which grape alone makes the dry white appellation wine of Kefalonia?
questions.exp: Robola of Kefalonia is Robola alone. Assyrtiko is Santorini's grape, Moschofilero is Mantinia's, and Vidiano is the rising white of Crete.

questions.q: In which sea does the island of Kefalonia lie?
questions.exp: Kefalonia is the largest of the Ionian islands, west of mainland Greece. Santorini and Samos are in the Aegean, Crete's south coast faces the Libyan Sea, and the Adriatic lies to the north beyond Corfu.

questions.q: What is the main soil of Kefalonia's Robola vineyards?
questions.exp: Robola grows on bare limestone scree and karst. Volcanic ash is Santorini's soil, schist marks the terraces of Samos, and granite plays no part in Kefalonia's vineyards.

questions.q: Which mountain rises above the Robola vineyards of Kefalonia?
questions.exp: Mount Ainos, over 1,600 metres and a national park of Kefalonian fir, rises above the Omala valley, the heart of Robola.

questions.q: Which style is Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia?
questions.exp: Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia is a fortified sweet red aged in cask, like its Patras cousin. The dry white is Robola, and a sun-dried sweet white would be Vinsanto or Samos Nectar.

questions.q: Which grape gives its name to the sweet white appellation of Kefalonia?
questions.exp: Muscat of Kefalonia is the island's sweet white PDO, from Muscat Blanc. The other two appellations are Robola of Kefalonia, the dry white, and Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia, a fortified sweet red.

questions.q: Which area of Kefalonia is the heart of Robola production?
questions.exp: The high Omala valley below Mount Ainos, home of the growers' cooperative, is Robola's heartland. Paliki and the Lixouri coast in the west are lower and warmer, and Argostoli is the capital on its bay.

regions.name: Samos
regions.summary: Samos, an island in the eastern Aegean barely two kilometres off the Turkish coast, is the great Greek name for sweet Muscat. Its one grape is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, locally Moschato Aspro, grown on stone terraces that climb Mount Ampelos to about 800 metres. One of Greece's oldest appellations, it makes sweet wine in several ways: Vin Doux, fortified early with spirit; Vin Doux Naturel and its Grand Cru, fortified after a partial fermentation; and Nectar, unfortified, from sun-dried grapes. A growers' union founded in 1934 makes most of it. Lord Byron called for Samian wine, and servers still pour it with dessert.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean, hot and dry in summer and mild and wet in winter, but greener than most Aegean islands because its mountains catch the rain. The north side, facing the sea and the summer northerlies, is cooler and moister; the south is hotter. Altitude matters most: the terraces climb from near sea level to about 800 metres, and the harvest is staggered over many weeks, from late summer on the coast to autumn high on the mountain, giving a wide range of ripeness on one small island.
terroir.soils: Poor, stony and well drained: schist across much of the mountain, with limestone, clay and sandy patches, all held in place by stone-walled terraces. The thin soils limit vigour and yield and concentrate the Muscat's perfume; the deeper ground near the coast gives larger crops and simpler wine.
terroir.topography: A mountainous island with two main massifs: Mount Ampelos, whose name means vine, in the centre and north, and the higher Mount Kerkis in the west, over 1,400 metres. The vineyards climb the northern and central slopes of Ampelos in narrow terraces, around villages such as Vourliotes and Manolates, and spread across the lower ground near Karlovasi in the west. The capital, Vathy, lies on a deep bay in the north-east.
terroir.water: The Aegean surrounds the island, and the narrow Mycale strait separates it from Turkey. Mountain streams and springs make the north of Samos unusually green, and sea breezes and altitude cool the terraces through the hot summer.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moschato Aspro, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, the only grape of the appellation: orange blossom, apricot, honey and grapey perfume, made fortified or from sun-dried grapes, young and fresh or long-aged and amber.

wines.note: The everyday classic: grape spirit added to the must at or near the start of fermentation, to about 15 per cent alcohol, very sweet and fresh, golden, with orange blossom, apricot and honey. Serve chilled with fruit tarts, baklava or cheese.

A Vin Doux Naturel from selected fruit of the best, higher vineyards, fermented partway and then fortified: more complex than the Vin Doux, with apricot, citrus peel, honey and spice and a cleaner, longer finish. Serve with blue cheese, foie gras or almond desserts.

Unfortified sweet wine from sun-dried Muscat, fermented to a natural stop and aged for several years in oak: amber, dried apricot, fig, raisin, caramel and spice, rich yet fresh. Serve with crème brûlée, bread pudding, nuts or chocolate.
Long cask-aged versions, the union's Anthemis the best known: amber, orange marmalade, toffee and nuts, a Greek cousin to an aged Muscat de Rivesaltes or a Rutherglen Muscat.
A modern sideline: Muscat fermented dry, floral and grapey with a bitter orange finish, a striking aperitif with meze and a lesson that Muscat smells sweet without being sweet.

made.viticulture: The vineyard is a work of stone: narrow terraces, the pezoules, built up the mountain over centuries, too steep and too small for machines, so everything is done by hand. Vines are mostly low bush vines, with newer plantings on wires on the gentler ground. Muscat Blanc is thin-skinned, prone to rot and to sunburn, and its compact bunches suffer in a wet autumn, so the higher, airier terraces are prized. Yields are low on the mountain and higher on the plain. Because the terraces climb from the coast to about 800 metres, the harvest runs for weeks, from the lowest vines in late summer to the highest in autumn, and the growers deliver their grapes to the union's wineries. Picking date sets the style: ripe fruit for the Vin Doux, the best fruit of the high terraces for the Grand Cru, and overripe fruit laid out in the sun for Nectar. The labour of the terraces, and the loss of growers to other work, is the vineyard's lasting threat.
made.winemaking: Samos makes sweet wine in three ways. For the Vin Doux, grape spirit is added to the must at or just after the start of fermentation, keeping almost all of the grape's sugar and raising the alcohol to about 15 per cent. For the Vin Doux Naturel and the Grand Cru, the must ferments partway before the spirit stops it, which gives a little more complexity. For Nectar, the Muscat is dried in the sun for days until the grapes shrivel, then fermented slowly without any spirit to a natural stop and aged in oak for several years. The young fortified wines are kept in tank for freshness; the long-aged wines, such as Anthemis, spend years in oak and turn amber. A small amount of Muscat is fermented dry for the modern dry white.

law.classification: Samos is one of Greece's oldest protected designations of origin, for sweet wine from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains grown on the island. Its categories carry the French terms the trade adopted for its export market: Vin Doux, fortified at or near the start of fermentation; Vin Doux Naturel, fortified after a partial fermentation, with Grand Cru for selected fruit of the best, higher vineyards; and Vin Naturellement Doux, the unfortified sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, sold as Nectar. The old OPE seal for sweet appellation wines covered it. The Union of Winemaking Cooperatives of Samos, founded in 1934, has long made most of the island's wine and owns its best-known labels.

places.name: Mount Ampelos
places.note: The central massif whose name means vine, terraced on its northern and central slopes up to about 800 metres: the heart of Samos Muscat and the source of its Grand Cru fruit.

places.name: Vourliotes
places.note: A mountain village on the northern slopes above the coast, amid some of the island's highest and most admired terraces.

places.name: Manolates
places.note: A village high on the northern side of Ampelos, whose terraces are among the coolest and latest to be picked.

places.name: Karlovasi and the west
places.note: The island's second town and port in the west, with vineyards on the lower slopes towards Mount Kerkis and on the coastal ground, where riper, earlier fruit grows.

places.name: Vathy
places.note: The capital and port on a deep bay in the north-east, the harbour from which the island's wine has long been shipped.

places.name: Mount Kerkis
places.note: The higher, rockier mountain in the west, over 1,400 metres, whose slopes carry fewer vines but shelter the western vineyards.

producers.name: Union of Winemaking Cooperatives of Samos (Samos Wines)
producers.why: Founded in 1934, the growers' union that makes most of the island's wine: the Vin Doux, the Grand Cru, Nectar, the long-aged Anthemis and a dry Muscat, the labels any server meets.

questions.q: Which grape makes the wines of the Samos appellation?
questions.exp: Samos is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Moschato Aspro, alone. Muscat of Alexandria is the Muscat of Lemnos, Moschofilero is Mantinia's unrelated grape, and Malvasia leads the sweet whites of Crete.

questions.q: Which Samos wine is made from sun-dried grapes without fortification?
questions.exp: Nectar is the unfortified Samos, from sun-dried Muscat aged in oak. Vin Doux, the Grand Cru and the long-aged Anthemis are all fortified with grape spirit.

questions.q: On which mountain do most of the vineyard terraces of Samos lie?
questions.exp: The terraces climb Mount Ampelos, whose name means vine, to about 800 metres. Kerkis is the higher western peak of Samos, Ainos is Kefalonia's mountain, and Ida is Crete's Psiloritis.

questions.q: What is the local Greek name for the Muscat grape of Samos?
questions.exp: Moschato Aspro, white Muscat, is the Greek name for Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, the only grape of the Samos appellation.

questions.q: Which country's coast lies closest to the island of Samos?
questions.exp: Samos lies in the eastern Aegean, separated from the Turkish coast by the narrow Mycale strait; it is not in the Cyclades with Santorini.

questions.q: Which French term on a Samos label means the Muscat was fortified partway through its fermentation?
questions.exp: Vin Doux Naturel, with its Grand Cru from the higher vineyards, ferments partway before grape spirit stops it. Plain Vin Doux is fortified at the start, and Vin Naturellement Doux, sold as Nectar, is not fortified at all.

questions.exp: Samos Grand Cru is a Vin Doux Naturel from selected fruit of the best, higher vineyards, fortified after a partial fermentation; it names no classified site, and noble rot plays no part.
